title: Characterizing and Optimizing Realistic Workloads on a Commercial Compute-in-SRAM Device
problem: Prior compute-in-SRAM evaluations rely on simulators or small prototypes, so the real-world performance and energy efficiency of commercial devices under realistic AI workloads (particularly retrieval-augmented generation over large corpora) is not well understood, and programming principles for exploiting the architecture's 2-million bit-processor parallelism are largely unknown.
motivation: Compute-in-SRAM architectures achieve massive on-chip bandwidth (26 TB/s on the GSI APU vs. 7 TB/s for A100 GPU) at far lower power, making them attractive for memory-bound AI workloads, but extracting this potential requires non-obvious data layout and movement optimizations that existing analytical models do not capture.
method: The paper characterizes the commercial GSI APU (2M 1-bit processors at 500 MHz, 25 TOPS, 26 TB/s on-chip bandwidth, 12MB L1 / 64KB L2 / 1MB L3 / 16GB DDR) using the Phoenix benchmark suite and matrix multiplication microbenchmarks, and develops a Python-based analytical framework modeling non-uniform data movement costs across 4 memory levels (L1-L4) and intra-VR vs. inter-VR operations. Three optimizations are proposed and validated on real hardware: (1) communication-aware reduction mapping that maps the reduction axis temporally to cheaper inter-VR operations (scalar-vector product) rather than costly intra-VR spatial reduction; (2) DMA coalescing via subgroup copy to eliminate redundant off-chip data duplication across loop iterations; and (3) broadcast-friendly data layouts that reduce L3 lookup table sizes from K*N to N elements to cut broadcast latency. These optimizations are applied to RAG retrieval over 10-200GB corpora.
key_novelty: First comprehensive real-hardware evaluation of a commercial compute-in-SRAM device (GSI APU) under realistic AI workloads, revealing that even compute-in-SRAM can be bandwidth-bound without careful data layout optimization, and demonstrating three concrete optimizations that approach the compute roofline.
contributions: First comprehensive real-hardware performance and energy characterization of a commercial compute-in-SRAM device (GSI APU) under Phoenix benchmarks, matrix multiplication, and RAG workloads
Analytical framework modeling non-uniform data movement costs and hierarchical reduction latencies for general-purpose compute-in-SRAM architectures
Three data movement and layout optimizations: communication-aware reduction mapping, DMA coalescing, and broadcast-friendly layouts
4.8x-6.6x retrieval speedup over CPU and GPU-matching latency for RAG at 54.4x-117.9x lower energy than NVIDIA A6000

metrics.speedup: 4.8x-6.6x retrieval speedup over optimized CPU; 1.1x-1.8x end-to-end RAG latency improvement; matches NVIDIA A6000 GPU latency for RAG
metrics.energy_or_tops_w: 54.4x-117.9x energy reduction vs. NVIDIA A6000 GPU for RAG; 41.8x speedup over CPU on Phoenix benchmarks

limitations: The off-chip (DDR4/HBM) memory bandwidth is modeled via simulation rather than measured; results apply to the specific GSI APU architecture and generalization to other compute-in-SRAM designs requires re-profiling the analytical framework.
primary_theme: Real-hardware compute-in-SRAM characterization and optimization for RAG
